howToRefresh: Ingest the KY History morning email to public/content/raw-briefs/YYYY-MM-DD.md, run npm run parse-briefs, then npm run build (includes build-home-preview). The homepage also re-reads stories.json in the browser.

stories.title: John Breckinridge of Cabell's Dale
stories.summary: John Breckinridge brought his family and 25 enslaved people from Virginia to Cabell's Dale near Lexington in 1793, carried Jefferson's secret Kentucky Resolutions through the legislature in 1798, and died Jefferson's attorney general in 1806.
stories.quote: In April 1793 John Breckinridge, a Virginia lawyer, stepped off a flatboat in Kentucky with his family and 25 enslaved people.

photo.title: Portrait of John Breckinridge
photo.credit: Alban Jasper Conant, 1863 · U.S. Department of Justice · public domain

stories.heroDeck: In April 1793 John Breckinridge, a Virginia lawyer, stepped off a flatboat in Kentucky with his family and 25 enslaved people.

stories.title: Greenville, a hilltop seat on William Campbell's land
stories.summary: Muhlenberg County was formed in 1798, and in 1799 Col. William Campbell gave 30 acres of high ground with two springs for its seat. Greenville got a log courthouse in 1800, a charter in 1812, the railroad in 1871, and then coal.
stories.quote: Greenville began with a gift of land on a hill.

photo.title: The Muhlenberg County Courthouse (1907) on the square in Greenville (photographed 2013)

stories.heroDeck: Greenville began with a gift of land on a hill.

stories.title: The Woman from Short Cave
stories.summary: Saltpeter miners found an ancient Native American woman's burial in Short Cave in the early 1810s. She was shown in Mammoth Cave, toured the East, went to the American Antiquarian Society in 1817 and the Smithsonian in 1876, and was later called Fawn Hoof.
stories.quote: Sometime between 1811 and 1813 (the accounts differ), as the country went to war with Britain, men digging saltpeter in Short Cave, in Edmonson County, opened a grave.

photo.title: AI illustration: imagined portrait of the Woman from Short Cave, an older Native woman of the prehistoric Eastern Woodlands, in deerskin and woven cloth, with a feather in her hair and bead and pendant necklaces; no known likeness exists.
photo.alt: AI illustration: imagined portrait of the Woman from Short Cave, an older Native woman of the prehistoric Eastern Woodlands, in deerskin and woven cloth, with a feather in her hair and bead and pendant necklaces; no known likeness exists.
photo.credit: AI illustration · Kentucky History Drive; no known likeness exists

stories.heroDeck: Sometime between 1811 and 1813 (the accounts differ), as the country went to war with Britain, men digging saltpeter in Short Cave, in Edmonson County, opened a grave.

stories.title: Black Hoof, the Shawnee warrior who chose peace
stories.summary: Black Hoof (Catecahassa), a Mekoche Shawnee born about 1740, fought Kentucky's settlers for decades, then led the Ohio Shawnee toward peace, farming and diplomacy. He kept most of his people out of Tecumseh's War and never signed a removal treaty.
stories.quote: Few men fought Kentucky's settlers longer than Catecahassa, the Shawnee the Americans called Black Hoof.

photo.title: Memorial to Black Hoof (Catahecassa) at Chief Blackhoof Memorial Park in Saint Johns, Ohio, where he died in 1831 (photographed 2021)

stories.heroDeck: Few men fought Kentucky's settlers longer than Catecahassa, the Shawnee the Americans called Black Hoof.

stories.title: Denmark and Gaines' Denmark, the Saddlebred's foundation
stories.summary: Denmark, a Kentucky Thoroughbred foaled in 1839, sired Gaines' Denmark in 1851, and their line became the core of the American Saddlebred. The breed's registry was founded in Louisville in 1891, and in 1908 it named Denmark its sole foundation sire.
stories.quote: Denmark, a Kentucky Thoroughbred, is the horse that turned the Kentucky Saddler into a breed.

photo.title: AI illustration: imagined portrait of Gaines' Denmark, a black saddle-type stallion with two white hind socks, standing in profile in the manner of 1850s American horse painting; no known likeness exists.
photo.alt: AI illustration: imagined portrait of Gaines' Denmark, a black saddle-type stallion with two white hind socks, standing in profile in the manner of 1850s American horse painting; no known likeness exists.
photo.credit: AI illustration · Kentucky History Drive; no known likeness exists

layers.name: Fort Boonesborough
layers.blurb: Daniel Boone’s 1775 settlement on the Kentucky River — Capital of the Colony of Transylvania.

layers.name: Big Bone Lick
layers.blurb: A Pleistocene salt lick where mastodons left bones in the mud — Kentucky’s window on deep time.

layers.name: Thomas D. Clark Center for Kentucky History
layers.blurb: Flagship Kentucky Historical Society museum, covering more than 12,000 years of the Commonwealth.

photo.title: Thomas D. Clark Center for Kentucky History
photo.attribution: Lee Wright · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0

layers.name: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace
layers.wiki: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace National Historical Park
layers.blurb: The Sinking Spring farm where Lincoln was born in 1809, plus the Knob Creek boyhood unit.

layers.name: Blue Licks Battlefield
layers.wiki: Blue Licks Battlefield State Resort Park
layers.blurb: August 19, 1782: the last major Revolutionary War battle in Kentucky.

layers.name: Old Talbott Tavern
layers.blurb: Court Square tavern since the late 1700s — among America’s oldest inns, still a working bourbon bar.

photo.title: Old Talbott Tavern, Bardstown
photo.attribution: Christopher L. Riley · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0

layers.name: Goddard Covered Bridge
layers.blurb: White Bridge: a Town-lattice span over Sand Lick Creek, among Kentucky’s surviving covered bridges.

photo.title: Goddard Covered Bridge
photo.attribution: Greg Hume · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 3.0

layers.name: Bourbon Iron Works
layers.blurb: Jacob Myers blew in a charcoal blast furnace here in 1791 — munitions for the early Commonwealth.

photo.title: Bourbon Iron Works (Slate Furnace)
photo.attribution: Jeff Bates · HABS / Library of Congress · Public domain

layers.name: The Kentucke Gazette
layers.blurb: Kentucky’s first newspaper, begun August 11, 1787 by John and Fielding Bradford.

photo.title: Kentucke Gazette printing house
photo.attribution: William Henry Perrin / Filson Club · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

layers.name: Cumberland Falls
layers.blurb: The “Niagara of the South,” and one of the few Western Hemisphere places a moonbow can appear.

photo.title: Cumberland Falls
photo.attribution: Aaron Vowels · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0

layers.name: Frankfort Cemetery
layers.blurb: Hilltop rural cemetery (1844) overlooking the capital — Daniel and Rebecca Boone were reinterred here.

photo.title: Frankfort Cemetery
photo.attribution: Sydney Poore & Russell Poore · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0

layers.name: Buffalo Trace Distillery
layers.blurb: A Kentucky River distilling campus with late-1700s roots, continuous through Prohibition.
